title: Moral Authority
author: Fabrizio Mejía Madrid
content:
_This article by[Fabrizio Mejía
Madrid](https://www.sinembargo.mx/author/fabriziomejia/) originally appeared
in the [September 4, 2026 edition of
SinEmbargo](https://www.sinembargo.mx/4864395/autoridad-moral/), a Mexican
independent news outlet._

> "_There is a political courage that does not come from ambitions but from
> convictions. It is what makes the difference between leaders and
> leadership._ "

In recent days we have heard much discussion of results and data regarding the
second year of Claudia Sheinbaum’s government. But we have not heard anyone
refer to what makes those successful results possible—in investment, wages,
labor poverty, security, infrastructure, and with the United States. It is
called moral authority. It is different from political authority and
legitimacy because it is not something measurable in millions of votes or in
approval ratings, although these are useful for us to see it.

We understand moral authority as the consistency between a person’s values and
their daily actions and attitudes. This coherence generates trust and respect
beyond mere obedience. Moral authority is not a legal matter; it is the
integrity of a person’s character. But when we speak of a President, that
character exists outside the laws or of simple institutional power. Its
weapons are persuasion, wisdom, and knowing how to lead by example. Moral
authority is the capacity to influence others through the way one lives. It is
not about personality, popularity, or technique. It arises from character. It
grows when a person constantly aligns their life with what they consider true
and good. Moral authority emerges when one acts for the good, even when it is
not convenient. That is why it is moral and not a calculation. In the two
examples we will look at—one of AMLO and another of Claudia—these are not
tactical decisions but decisions of conviction. As Cicero wrote: “If power is
by nature indivisible, there must exist something external to it that limits
it.” That role is morality, the distinction between good and evil.

But first its political dimension. When this moral authority enters into a
relationship with citizens, a space of shared values is created where honesty,
justice, and treatment among equals are the substance, not just the form. The
display of those shared values in a public space is an ethical commitment.
There, there are no linguistic constructions or media manipulations.

It was López Obrador who was able to bring this type of authority to the
Presidency of the Republic. As a leader of the opposition he was consistent
between words and deeds, which he called his maxims: “Do not lie, do not
steal, do not betray the people.” Once in the National Palace he continued to
preserve that integrity between values, way of governing, and character, which
renewed the trust of many more than had originally voted for him. “Love is
repaid with love” was the slogan he found to reflect that relationship of
political trust in the democratic sphere.

The former president who preceded him, Enrique Peña Nieto, utterly lacked
integrity and, therefore, depended on publicity to be regarded as a ruler.
From the financing of the PRI campaign that brought him to the Presidency
through the purchase of five million votes, he entered into collusion with
Odebrecht, the Spanish electricity companies, and with Israel’s espionage-
equipment services, through his crony Avishai Neria, with whom he was
photographed this week at a wedding in Portofino, Italy—at the wedding of
another of the Israeli partners in Mexico, the singer Omer Adam. Peña Nieto
had denied knowing Neria and Uri Emanuel Ansbacher, who sold to Tomás Zerón
and to several governors, and even to private individuals—allegedly to Isabel
Miranda de Wallace—the Pegasus system for infiltrating cell phones. Peña
denied it when it appeared in Tel Aviv’s The Marker, but now he was filmed
alongside Neria at a wedding.

It was not only lying that prevented Peña Nieto from having a gram of moral
authority. It was his television contract, the sacks of money he spent on
self-promotion, and the fact that he was the puppet of a group of businessmen,
such as Claudio X. González. When he was no longer useful to those businessmen
who were going to earn billions both at the Texcoco airport and on the Mexico
City–Querétaro train that was cancelled, they let Peña Nieto fall into
disgrace by disclosing that the house he lived in was part of a bribe. He
could not defend himself. He had no authority of any kind, neither moral nor
political. There remains the photo in which José Andrés de Oteyza, director of
OHL, scolds him in public. As for the one before Peña, Felipe Calderón, we
won’t even go there. He was capable of leading a massacre that exceeded even
his six-year term just to legitimize himself in an office obtained through
fraud. He was capable of saying that one part of Mexicans should die so that
the other could live in peace. And he calls himself a Catholic. But let us not
even speak of the one who lied by saying he was protecting the national
interest when all he did was defend the Sinaloa Cartel and the policies of the
DEA.

By definition, morality and authority stand at opposite ends of the space of
social relations. Morality concerns correct conduct—the distinction between
right and wrong apart from the power of the Law—while authority implies the
faculty to decide, order, and make others obey. But, since moral authority is
a political and not a legal consideration, obedience can turn not only into
approval but into open support to take part. This was especially notable when,
between January 9 and 15, 2019, López Obrador ordered the closing of Petróleos
Mexicanos’s pipelines to stop the illegal extraction of gasoline and asked
motorists for patience. Waiting in line for gasoline was understood as an act
of political participation to help the government combat theft. At that
moment, the President reached an approval level of 80 percent. This did not
only mean that people approved of stopping the so-called huachicol, but that
they recognized in AMLO the moral authority to carry it out. That is why the
opposition’s brilliant ruse has been to try to link López Obrador, his
collaborators, his fellow countrymen, and even his children precisely with the
issue that brought him the most support. They have not been able to, because
of the moral authority he still has, even far from the public arena.

For her part, President Sheinbaum obtained her highest approval level—83
percent—in May 2025, when she debuted the slogan “Cooperation without
subordination.” Some 53 percent declared themselves ready to defend the
country, while 71 percent rejected any kind of interference from the United
States. Her moral authority came, then, from not bowing her head before a more
powerful adversary. This would have been expected from the PRIAN, but not from
the left. Cunning in the face of the powerful is a cultural value throughout
the country. The space of shared values includes, besides honesty and the
dispensing of justice, also temperance and dignity. That attitude of not
provoking the advantaged adversary but also not yielding in the defense of our
national sovereignty coincided with a set of shared cultural values in Mexican
society, such as defensive patriotism, cultural resistance in the face of a
far greater power, and the activation of community cohesion. What moves those
values is that the dignity of Mexicans cannot be negotiable, above all in a
situation where the main aggressor is the greatest economic and military power
on the planet. There, temperance and firmness—Sheinbaum’s “cool head”—were the
glue of adherence to her moral authority. The defense of the Nation’s
strategic interests was attacked by the PRIAN once again as it declared itself
ready to receive the armed forces of the United States, their agents of the
CIA, the DEA, and even ICE, or making a pilgrimage to Washington to plead for
help in the face of a catastrophe that excites only them. They were wrong
again, because Claudia has moral authority.

Moral authority is not only spoken, it is exercised. It is consistency of
actions, behaviors, and even of the character’s style. A ruler faithful to
themselves generates trust to act. But a ruler who is, moreover, consistent
with what the people expect of him or her has moral authority. That is why I
believe that both the President and the new leadership of her party have
insisted in recent days on honesty. Not only to preserve moral authority, but
because it is a value tied to prosperity. One need only look at the times of
Peña Nieto, when corruption was said to be “cultural,” at how the budget never
sufficed for the well-being of the majority. With honesty as a way of life and
austerity—not of the workers but of the government—historic distributions of
social justice have been achieved. Honesty and doing good are two values that
have proven to be part of a majority of Mexicans. Theft and plunder, conflict
of interest, nepotism, and influence-peddling must be publicly condemned when
practiced by rulers and businessmen. But there still remains the horizon of
condemning greed as a way of life, one of the burdens of neoliberalism and of
the concentration of enormous fortunes in a single family. If there is
morality in the exercise of politics, it should also exist in the realm of
business.

From Salinas de Gortari to Peña Nieto—that is, the entire period of the
neoliberal PRIAN—it was said that morality was not a public matter but only a
private one, and that everything was very relative when it came to
distinguishing good from evil. When rulers and businessmen were caught in some
swindle, they always said it was legal, because indeed decency as a dimension
of public affairs is not something constitutional, but a matter of the
expectation of the governed.

The bond established between rulers and the ruled on the basis of public
virtues is what makes moral authority a political matter and not a religious
or private one. It does not descend from the heavens, whether divine or
presidential. Nor is it shut away behind the doors of homes. It is a space of
public encounter of values as universal as honesty, justice, equality,
prosperity, and happiness in community. The consistencies between the two and,
in turn, with the President’s conduct have generated moral authority, a kind
of affection that is political.

There is a political courage that does not come from ambitions but from
convictions. It is what makes the difference between leaders and leadership,
between managers of an administration or conductors of a Nation. The two
examples I have given—when both AMLO and Claudia have had almost total
approval levels—have to do with that character: adjusting particular interests
to the general interest, and being brave. It is not the arrogance of Lorenzo
Córdova. It is not the thuggery of “Alito” Moreno. Nor is it dressing up as a
soldier with the sleeves hanging, or wearing boots and a hat, or chewing gum.
It is moral courage. And it is understanding that, at this moment, elections
will not be about competence, but about convictions, ideology, and values
shared with the people. In sum, they will be about moral authority.
